progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: Stage 5 Science (measurement, units, forces as pushes and pulls); Stage 5 Mathematics (Pythagoras; SI units; rates such as km h⁻¹). No earlier video.
progression.startsWith: A car drives one lap of a four hundred metre test track, and stops where it started. How far has it travelled? Four hundred metres. Now, how far is it from where it started? Zero. Both answers are right, because they answer different questions. The first one doesn't care which way the car went. The second one depends on it completely. That difference, whether direction matters, splits the quantities we use to describe motion into two kinds.
progression.stopsAfter: magnitude, scalar and vector defined; distance against displacement and speed against velocity explained on visible cases; acceleration shown to be a vector; time a scalar; all six classified with the "which way?" test. No vector addition, angles, components or sign conventions.
progression.nextLesson: v02, vector diagrams: how two vectors add tip to tail to give a resultant, or subtract to give a difference.

teaching.task: *A car drives one lap of a 400 m test track and stops where it started. It has travelled 400 m, but it is no distance at all from the start. How can both be true, and which quantities in motion need a direction?*
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a size alone does not fix an outcome; direction completes it (1, 2); (2) distance adds every metre of path, so it only grows (1, 3); (3) displacement is the start-to-finish arrow, so bends and returns shorten it (3 to 5); (4) speed is a dial reading; velocity also says which way, so it decides where you end up (6); (5) acceleration is how velocity changes; its direction decides speeding up or slowing down (7); (6) turning changes velocity even at constant speed (8); (7) time has no direction in space (9); (8) the units don't decide, the direction does (10); (9) memory aid (11).
teaching.conversationalApproach: A car drives one lap of a four hundred metre test track, and stops where it started. Suppose I tell you a drone is five metres from its launch pad. The first pair is distance and displacement. Quick prediction.
teaching.openingDecision: cold open, no title card. Plan view of a coded oval test track (two grey lane lines, a chequered start line on the bottom straight, a navy start pin "start"), compass top right; the top-view blue car plate sits on the start line, facing right. On "track" the car drives one lap anticlockwise (about 6 s, constant pace) with the route tracer: the amber trail draws behind it and an amber counter in the right column "distance travelled" ticks 0 to 400 m; at the same time a thin navy arrow from the start pin to the car grows, swings round with the car (longest at the far straight) and shrinks back. On "metres" the counter settles at "400 m" and pulses. On "Zero" the car is back on the start pin; the navy arrow has shrunk to nothing; a navy readout writes "distance from start: 0 m". On the fourth sentence the two readouts sit side by side with tags "ignores direction" (amber) and "depends on direction" (navy) written on "doesn't care" and "depends". On "kinds" the heading writes on: "Scalars and vectors: when does direction matter?" and the two readouts slide up as two column headers in waiting (empty).
teaching.understandingCheck: Quick prediction. Here are three drone trips. Four east, then three north. Three east, then three back west. Four east, then three more east. On which trip is the size of the displacement equal to the distance? Have a think. Your turn. A drone flies six point zero metres east, then eight point zero metres north. Calculate the distance it travels and the magnitude of its displacement, and explain why the two values are different. Pause here to answer. Last one. A ferry goes two point zero kilometres north, then returns two point zero kilometres south to the same wharf, at a steady fifteen kilometres per hour. A passenger says its velocity was the same on both legs. Find the distance and displacement, and explain whether the passenger is right. Pause here to answer.
